title: Spatial Navigation and Negative Emotions: The Effect of Emotion Processing on Wayfinding and Visuospatial Working Memory
research_question: This dissertation investigates how negative emotional information (facial expressions, body expressions, contextual scenes) affects spatial navigation abilities (wayfinding, navigation domains) and visuospatial working memory, considering gender differences and the specific effects of fear versus anger.

participants.description: Across five experiments, participants were university students and Prolific Academic users, aged 18-60, from Italy and UK, English speakers.
participants.recruitment: university recruitment website, snowball sampling, campus and outside advertising, Prolific Academic platform

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Customized multi-storey office building virtual environment (4 floors) for navigation tasks, presented via Oculus Rift S or Oculus Quest 2 headsets.
30 male and 30 female frontal faces expressing neutral, fearful, or angry emotions from Radboud Faces Database (Experiment 1).
30 male and 30 female bodies expressing neutral, fear, or angry emotions with blurred faces from Bochum Emotional Stimulus Set (BESST) (Experiment 2).
60 pictures of threatening and reassuring contextual scenes (15 city, 15 nature in each category), without human elements (Experiment 3).
Two-minute video recording of an avatar navigating a virtual 'office building' from a first-person perspective (Experiment 4).
90 faces (neutral, fear, anger) from Max Plank Face Database (half male, half female, 3 age categories) for gender categorization task (Experiment 4).
Backward Corsi Block Tapping Task (CBT) with 9 blue squares (Experiment 5).
Delayed Non-Match to Sample Task (DNMS) with an array of seven faces (neutral, fearful, angry) from Max Planck Face Database (Experiment 5).

mechanisms: Learning and familiarity in repeated navigation tasks
Gender differences in spatial navigation strategies (e.g., survey vs. landmark-based)
Evolutionarily based behavioral responses (approach/avoidance, fight/flight) elicited by threatening stimuli
Prioritization of threat detection due to social information from faces
Nature of threat (immediate/directed vs. unidentified/broader) influencing subsequent navigation
Emotional contagion affecting individual's emotional experience and navigation performance
Competition for shared visuospatial working memory (VSWM) cognitive resources between emotion processing and spatial tasks
Gender differences in managing VSWM resources for emotional face processing
Emotion regulation strategies differing between genders
Cognitive load imposed by processing emotional faces
moderators: Emotion type (fear vs. anger vs. neutral)
Stimulus type (faces vs. bodies vs. scenes)
Spatial navigation domain (landmark, location, path knowledge)
Task complexity (e.g., route ordering vs. directional pointing)
implementation_implications: Improve training programs and design realistic simulation scenarios for professions requiring spatial navigation and emotional regulation (e.g., firefighting, military)
Develop virtual reality-based exposure therapies with emotional and social stimuli for clinical psychology (e.g., PTSD, anxiety, phobias)
Inspire development of early diagnostic tools for neurodegenerative diseases (e.g., Alzheimer's) using navigation and emotion processing tasks

limitations: Virtual reality environment was limited to a small-scale closed environment (office building), potentially affecting generalisability to larger outdoor environments.
Sample sizes in some experiments (e.g., Experiment 2) were small and unbalanced, limiting inference and statistical power.
Data collected from samples of different ages across experiments (e.g., mean age ~20 in Exp 1-4, ~40 in Exp 5), potentially introducing inconsistencies.
Emotional stimuli were presented as static images on a two-dimensional screen, which may have limited the sense of presence and realism compared to dynamic or multimodal stimuli.
Lack of attention-related behavioral measures (e.g., eye tracking) to understand attentional patterns during spatial tasks.
Emotional stimuli were task-irrelevant, which may limit their influence compared to task-relevant emotions according to appraisal theory.
Focus only on negative emotional expressions, not positive ones (except for reassuring contexts in Exp 3).
